leads.text: Fail-open sanitizer policy in the highest-centrality chokepoint `initializeOptions` (lib/sanitize.js:14 and :18): the guards `options.allowedTags.length > 0` and `Object.keys(options.allowedAttributes).length > 0` mean that a developer who passes the most restrictive policy -- `allowedTags: []` ("strip ALL tags") or `allowedAttributes: {}` ("allow NO attributes") -- has that policy SILENTLY DISCARDED: `sanitizerOptions` is left as the empty object `{}` built at line 13. That `{}` is then passed as the 2nd argument to every `sanitizeHtml(...)` call (lines 37, 42, 57), and sanitize-html 2.x merges options over `sanitizeHtml.defaults`, so the empty object resolves to sanitize-html's PERMISSIVE DEFAULT allowlist (``, ``, ``, ``, headings, lists, tables, ...) instead of the developer's deny-everything policy. Attacker-controlled strings from req.body / req.query / req.params / req.headers therefore flow into `sanitizeHtml` under a materially weaker policy than the application configured, and HTML/attribute injection survives sanitization. The inverted condition is the defect: an explicitly-empty allowlist must be honoured as "allow nothing", not treated as "unset".

leads.text: `req.params` is listed as sanitized but the sanitization is a guaranteed no-op, leaving URL path parameters attacker-controlled and unsanitized downstream. index.js:7 iterates `['body','params','headers']` and does `req[k] = sanitize(req[k], options)` at index.js:9. When this middleware is installed globally as `app.use(xss())` (the documented usage, and the only shape the EntryPoint graph shows), the Express router has not yet matched the route layer, so `req.params` is still `{}` -- route params for `/:id` are populated by the router immediately before invoking the matched handler, i.e. AFTER this middleware already ran. `if (req[k])` passes because `{}` is truthy, so `sanitize({})` runs, iterates zero keys at lib/sanitize.js:51, and returns the same empty object -- producing a silent false sense of coverage. Consequently `req.params.*` reaches application handlers with raw attacker HTML/script, despite 'params' appearing in the sanitized list.

Object property NAMES are never sanitized -- only property values. In the object branch of `sanitize` (lib/sanitize.js:51-60), `Object.keys(data).forEach((key) => { ... data[key] = sanitizeHtml(item, ...) })` sanitizes the VALUE `item = data[key]` and writes it back under the ORIGINAL, unsanitized `key`. An attacker who controls JSON body / query-string property names (e.g. POST body `{"": "ok"}`, or query `?=1`) has that payload pass through the sanitizer completely untouched and reach the application inside `req.body` / `req.query`. Any app that renders object keys (key/value tables, form builders, `Object.keys(...)` loops in a template, error messages echoing field names) gets stored/reflected XSS despite the middleware being installed. The same gap applies to the `allowedKeys` skip at line 52, which additionally exempts an entire subtree from sanitization when its key matches.

Attacker-triggerable synchronous throw on deeply nested input: lib/sanitize.js:33-34 does `if (currentDepth > options.maxDepth) throw new Error(...)`, where `maxDepth` defaults to MAX_DEPTH=100 (lib/sanitize.js:5, 24-26). The recursion is driven directly by attacker-controlled structure -- `req.body` parsed by `express.json()` has no depth cap, so a request body nested >101 levels deep makes `sanitize` (recursing at lines 45 and 59) throw from inside the middleware on EVERY such request. This converts any request with deeply-nested JSON into an unconditional error-handler/500 path with no rate limit or recovery, and the thrown Error message interpolates `options.maxDepth`, leaking the configured sanitizer depth to the client if the app echoes error messages. Note this is a bounded-cost DoS (recursion is capped at 101 frames, so no stack exhaustion) -- the issue is the unhandled-rejection/500 amplification and the fail-closed-by-exception design rather than memory blowup.

leads.text: The depth guard in sanitize() raises an exception on attacker-controlled input, and no try/catch exists anywhere in the package to contain it. A request whose JSON body nests deeper than maxDepth (default MAX_DEPTH = 100) makes sanitize() throw out of the middleware body; because the throw happens inside the ['body','params','headers'].forEach callback, it also aborts sanitization of the remaining surfaces and skips next(). The guard fails closed (the request errors rather than passing unsanitized), but it hands any unauthenticated client a cheap, reliable way to force an error-handler path on every request.

leads.text: The middleware guards each surface with a bare truthiness test `if (req[k])` and silently does nothing when the value is falsy, with no warning and no fail-closed behaviour. If xss() is mounted before the body parser (app.use(xss()) before app.use(express.json())), req.body is undefined at middleware time, the guard is false, sanitization is skipped, and the body parsed moments later reaches route handlers completely unsanitized -- while the app appears correctly protected. The package ships no ordering assertion or diagnostic to detect this misregistration.
leads.evidence: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='index.js' ... ORDER BY line,col -> uid 708db725d150116e2dfb0d67fe6730d6a30cf237 `req[k]` (<operator>.indexAccess, line 8, column 10) is the sole guard, and the only sanitize call for these surfaces, uid 97c7dd9346b8d0317370ceb24fd3e6221e217d8a `sanitize(req[k], options)` (line 9), sits inside it. Source via semantic_search (index.js:7-26) confirms: `if (req[k]) { req[k] = sanitize(req[k], options); }` with no else branch. Contrast: req.query at line 12 (uid 2215dbd046b3fe2f377fea0e2e6d99dde5931eac) is sanitized unconditionally, showing the guard is specific to body/params/headers.

leads.text: In initializeOptions, three of the four option validators carry an explicit type guard but the `allowedAttributes` validator's guard is missing — it is validated only by hasOwn() + Object.keys(...).length, with no Array.isArray/object check, unlike its siblings allowedTags (Array.isArray), allowedKeys (Array.isArray) and maxDepth (typeof === 'number'). The inconsistency is the signal: an omitted/removed validation. Consequence: initializeOptions({allowedAttributes: null}) (or any non-object primitive) makes Object.keys(null) throw a TypeError, and because initializeOptions is the highest-centrality node in the reachable graph (0.00497) and runs on every single request through prepareSanitize, the throw aborts sanitization for all traffic rather than failing safe.

leads.text: Components-with-known-vulnerabilities: `sanitize-html` is declared as `~2.13.0`, and it is the SOLE XSS defense in this package — attacker-controlled request data reaches it at three confirmed reachable call sites (lib/sanitize.js:37 hop=1, :42 hop=2, :57 hop=2), all resolving to the external method node `sanitize-html` (is_external=true, reachable_from_entry=true). The tilde range caps resolution at `>=2.13.0 <2.14.0`, so any security fix published in 2.14.x or later is structurally un-installable without a manifest edit; there is no lockfile in the scan (only index.js and lib/sanitize.js are CpgFile nodes) so the exact resolved patch cannot be pinned down from the graph. This dependency warrants a version-level CVE review (sanitize-html's 2.x line has a history of allowlist-bypass and ReDoS advisories), and the pin should be widened to `^2` so patch/minor security releases are picked up. Flagged as a manifest/pattern-in-data issue — it does not depend on any single request flow.

leads.text: Components-with-known-vulnerabilities / stale-manifest: `body-parser` is declared `^1.19.0` while `express` is declared `^5.0.1`. Two problems in this literal pair: (1) the 1.x body-parser line's declared floor (1.19.0) predates the fixes in 1.20.x, including the high-severity urlencoded-extended resource-exhaustion DoS fixed in 1.20.3 — anything that honors the floor rather than re-resolving is exposed; (2) Express 5 already bundles its own body-parser 2.x internally, so a top-level `^1.19.0` declaration is a stale duplicate that pulls a second, older copy of the body parser into the tree. Because no lockfile is present in the scan, the actually-installed version cannot be read from the graph and must be checked against the manifest. This matters here specifically because body-parser is what materializes the attacker-controlled `req.body` object that this middleware then walks and mutates.

leads.text: Unbounded-recursion via an unvalidated numeric literal: `initializeOptions` accepts any caller-supplied `maxDepth` that passes only `typeof options.maxDepth === 'number' && options.maxDepth > 0` (lib/sanitize.js:25). Both `Infinity` and `Number.MAX_VALUE` satisfy that predicate, so `maxDepth` can be set to a value the guard `currentDepth > options.maxDepth` (lib/sanitize.js:33) can never exceed, disabling the depth ceiling entirely and leaving the mutual recursion `sanitize(options, item, currentDepth + 1)` (lib/sanitize.js:45 and :59) bounded only by the V8 call stack — a RangeError/stack-overflow on sufficiently nested input. There is no integer/finite check and no upper clamp against the `MAX_DEPTH = 100` literal declared at lib/sanitize.js:5; `MAX_DEPTH` is used only as the fallback when the predicate fails, never as a maximum. Reachability note: this is config-supplied rather than request-supplied in the bundled middleware, but index.js:23-25 exports `sanitize` (prepareSanitize) directly as a public API, so an integrator who forwards request-influenced options into it exposes the gap.

leads.text: Attacker-triggerable exception from the depth literal: with the default `MAX_DEPTH = 100` (lib/sanitize.js:5), `sanitize` responds to over-deep input by `throw new Error(`Maximum sanitization depth of ${options.maxDepth} exceeded`)` (lib/sanitize.js:34) rather than by truncating or dropping the branch. The reachable throw site is confirmed (line 34 reach=true), as is the taint entry: `sanitize(req.query, options)` carries a FLOWS_TO self-loop, marking its argument as already attacker-tainted.

leads.text: End-of-life / outdated development toolchain declared in the manifest: `eslint ^7.20.0` (ESLint 7 reached end-of-life and no longer receives security fixes; current major is far ahead), `prettier ^2.2.1` (superseded by 3.x), `chai ^4.2.0` (superseded by 5.x), `eslint-config-prettier ^7.2.0`, `eslint-plugin-prettier ^3.3.1`, `eslint-config-airbnb-base ^14.2.1`, `eslint-plugin-import ^2.22.1` and `supertest ^6.0.1`. These are build/test-time only and are not reachable from any request flow, so runtime exploitability is nil; they matter as supply-chain surface (an unmaintained lint/format plugin tree is a known vector for install-time compromise, and the eslint-config-prettier line in particular has been the subject of a published npm account-takeover incident in its 8.x/9.x/10.x branches). Low priority relative to the runtime `sanitize-html` pin; listed for completeness of the components-with-known-vulnerabilities sweep.
